I’m of two minds about this. 

For starters, fear-mongering about alcohol is alarmist and unscientific. (So “no amount” is safe? Not even a teaspoon? A milliliter? Please.) 

And that’s to say nothing about reporting on relative versus absolute risk, or the risks associated with processed food, or houses built before the 1970s, or many other things.  And no — no, no, no — not everyone who drinks is an alcoholic, or on the cusp of becoming one. That’s another laughably unscientific claim that just seethes with moral judgment. 

But yes, sure, alcohol is a drug — a high-risk, high-cost one that should be used thoughtfully, if you’re into it at all— and no one should have a drug pushed on them, let alone one that could impair them when driving a 5,000-pound machine near other people. 

We owe this industry absolutely nothing. We owe no industry anything at all.

The American Civil War was referred to as a civil war even before the war began. Once the war began, it was described as a civil war by US citizens and newspapers to describe the conflict as a war between components of one country.

The government of the Union used the term "War of the Rebellion", while Confederates used "the War for Southern Independence." Both terms had a propaganda element, of course.

The first major historical work about the war, written by John Abbott and published in the immediate aftermath (1866) was   titled "The History of the Civil War in America."

In the 1890s, as the US moved toward increased reconciliation, media in both the north and south increasingly used the term "Civil War" in referring to the conflict.

The 1907 Joint Resolution No. 41 passed by Congress recognized the term "Civil War" as the official designation of the war.

It seems to me wiser to maintain a more neutral and accurate term (civil war simply means a conflict between factions within one political entity, like a country), than revert to regionalized, politicized labels.

So the questions to ask are which people, and how? What were the political structures of these places, who held the power, and how did those people use it? 

So when we ask these questions, we stop thinking of the South and its components as monolithic political entities, and we start remembering how contentious secession really was. Several slave states refused to secede. Virginia split in two over the issue, and Tennessee nearly did. Most southern states raised at least one unit to fight for the Union.

Which is all why Slaveholders Rebellion is an excellent term. Not because it emphasizes rebellion, but because it redirects our focus away from abstractions or sentiment and towards the actual people who engineered  secession in the first place.

Lots of people saying that the LW should tell the wife, for the wife's "own good." It's clear from the questions the LW is (finally) asking that the wife probably doesn't know.   

If the LW is *genuinely* concerned about the wife, the she should pressure the husband to tell his wife about the affair, and demand proof that he has done so. ( The LW has several levers at her disposal, including an ultimatum that she will tell the wife if he doesn't provide proof.)

Betrayal trauma is a real thing, and the trauma is significantly worse when the betrayed partner learns about it from a stranger, and then must accuse the husband herself then sort through with his denials, defenses, and trickle-truths, while simultaneously processing her own betrayal trauma.  

Essentially, telling the wife does the cheaters dirty work for him, and uses the wife as an instrument of revenge.  Use what little leverage you have to make him do the right thing, and tell his wife directly.

That being said, I'm intrigued by the sentence, "You’re not obliged to prosecute the case merely because he deserves prosecution." It's a pretty turn of phrase, but perhaps questionable as an ethical principle. It might seem okay to bow out of accountability in this case, which ostensibly impacts a small number of people, but it doesn't hold up well when considering broader applications. There are many circumstances in which the existence of a party that deserves prosecution creates some level of ethical obligation to participate in that prosecution.

It's a tricky thing--deciding whether or not to tell his wife. I always think deep down people know, but advice columns are full of letters from people whose problem mostly stems from avoiding at all costs anything resembling conflict or confrontation. We often don't like to face and work out problems and in our magical thinking, just hope it will all get better, somehow.

I will share a story though. A friend of mine was married for a couple of decades to a serial womanizer. With one particular woman, it was so obvious that the attraction was palpable: it was if each was a sunflower bathing in each other's sun. But still my friend stayed. When she asked me for my advice over and over, I said, you cannot forgive someone who never do anything wrong. It got to the point where she had to take anxiety meds to go home. 

He told the girlfriend his wife had a gun, was crazy, and he as afraid to get a divorce. In the meantime, he gaslighted my friend, accusing her of adultery with the girlfriend's husband. When the girlfriend was divorced, he paid her rent.

But when it became obvious that he liked the drama of more than one woman (and there were quite a few), the girlfriend in a vengeful mood boxed up every card (his handwriting, but no signature), the promissory note he signed agreeing to pay the gf's rent if she'd move back to town, printed out emails.

And presented with the evidence, my friend did what she should have done years before: she left him and is happier now.

If the wind was just right, which it always seemed to be, the dense Grey smoke would drift across backwards in our direction. So thick and foul smelling we'd have to hide inside our house with the windows closed. We had a swimming pool and they ruined several family gatherings. They actually arrived with a fire truck and fire chief vehicle and, after stretching out a hose, doused the offending fire with a huge stream of water. Mother Bucka's and longtime friends. 

I graduated high school more than 50 years ago. I came from a poor working class family. Left Illinois to go "out West" by myself. I knew no one. Youth and ignorance ensured my bravery.  Became a lawyer, started my career, got married, had my daughter, and was well into my life. 

In those days there was no internet. For poor kids like me, long distance calls were only for emergencies. I lost touch with nearly all my high school friends, except a few pen pals. For those of us who far moved away, this was how life was. 

About fifteen years ago a colleague asked me to reach out to someone in another firm that she thought might be interested in joining the state bar committee we were on. I looked at the name and thought it was familiar. The surname wasn't common. I looked up the woman's photo on the firm's website, and I knew I had found the girl who had been my partner on our high school debate team in 1971! I recalled her as much more ladylike than I was, and that she needed a little more starch in her if she was going to debate all those tough high school boys from other schools. I called her and we arranged to have dinner.

Fast forward to the present - we're dear friends and see each other every few weeks. She told me she'd heard from mutual acquaintances that I'd become a lawyer, and that motivated her to do the same. Wow. I had no idea. But she is still much more ladylike and proper than I am.

Best to everyone this morning,
OC

As a Big Law lawyer, I can say with certainty that it is disingenuous to portray any Big Law (or smaller) corporate law firm as somehow strongly committed to social justice.  These are and have always been profit-seeking enterprises, and the tensions between those who would do more and less pro bono work is not new.  There are individuals in these firms, like in any company, who care deeply about specific issues and do their best to use their privileged position to do good.  

After all, today's civil rights litigation could not exist without Big Law; they could also not exist without the amazing and dedicated lawyers at the non-profits.  But those same non-profits rely on the Big Law firms precisely because many cases are too expensive and require too much person-power for smaller firms, a problem that gets worse as the federal judiciary becomes more hostile to civil rights.

That said, without the hyperbole in this investigative piece, the details of which are fascinating, it goes without saying that Paul Weiss went from being a Big Law firm with a small conscience to one with almost none.

Just like the professional rules of ethics (mostly) bar lawyers from sharing profits with non-lawyers, maybe it is time to ban litigators from sharing profits with corporate lawyers.

comments.name: B Satva
comments.body:
Certitude is not certainty. I don't doubt your belief is genuinely held & as such has powerful benefits to you. It's why we see the word "superpower" applied so often these days. We're looking for something beyond ourselves, supernatural, not only to save us but to validate OUR  worthiness. In this case the superpower of recognizing the superpower in your pet. In another era you would be called a mystic--recognizing something transcendent  in the quotidian. 

But there seems to be something else going on in our society with pets, in particular. They are serving some need to believe not only in specialness but also in innocence. Kind of like our obsession with the child prodigy -- endowed with special powers AND innocent. This way of approaching the mundane says something about us, of course. Perhaps we're truly finding the amazing in our human worlds with "beginners mind", or perhaps we're projecting our need to feel--and broadcast--OUR own specialness. 

I wonder if AI relationships serve a similar function. I think AI is a pet for people who aren't "dog people" or "cat people" but are experiencing the same needs & seeking to have them met externally. To feel special, to feel adored, no ulterior motives, no competition, control in the relationship, no ghosting or bad break ups. Less precariousness, less anxiety and fear (notice how we have as a society instrumentalized our pets into SUPPORT for dealing with OUR unpleasant emotions and feelings). 

At what unintended cost?

The excerpt that's available fascinates me -- it's from a dog's perspective, yes (I love the "triangles" of his mother's ears) but with a fully human vocabulary. comments.body: Unfortunately, it is my anecdotal observation that the number of fireflies has greatly reduced over the past decade.  My belief is that this is due to the use of Neonicotinoid based insecticides that have been applied to lawns in order to control grubs.  While this chemical has been banned in many locations (Europe & some US regions) it is very prevalent in most of the country.  It does work "all season" to control grubs, but firefly larvae are grubs and they are killed along with the "bad" bugs.  Personally, I don't use the stuff and can live with a lawn that is not perfect, but many (most?) homeowners and lawn maintenance companies apply it each year.  The chemical gets everywhere and runs off into small streams and ponds which is why small amphibians like "peeper frogs" are also in decline as it particularly harmful to those types of creatures.

All these apps and gadgets do is cause parents (especially new parents) more stress and anxiety. Worse yet, they charge you a subscription and collect your data for the privilege. 

I'm no luddite when it comes to parenting. It has its place and can be useful. For example, I self-hosted an app to track feedings so my wife and I could more easily stay aligned on which twin ate when.

However, these "AI" this sleep monitoring technologies don't really serve a purpose. Anecdotally, the only things I've heard about them from my friends who did try them were complaints. Things like false alarms waking them up in the middle of the night terrified only to find out an O2 sock had come off or a breathing sensor belt had slipped.

There's no evidence this type of monitoring does any good or prevent any harm. Your pediatrician isn't going to recommend using it. So what's the purpose? Just use an old fashioned sound or video monitor and follow safe sleep guidelines and you'll be fine.

As we watch fire weather increasing at alarming rates around the world we might consider the following.

Accelerating climate impacts: The frequency and intensity of extreme weather events, rising sea levels, and other climate-related disruptions are intensifying at an alarming rate.

Energy transition timeline: A complete overhaul of our energy infrastructure to renewable sources will take decades, even with significant global cooperation and investment.

Momentum in Earth's energy system: The climate system has a considerable amount of inertia, meaning that even if we drastically reduce emissions, it will take time for the planet to respond.

The combination of these factors could lead to:
Mass displacement: Rising sea levels and extreme weather events will force millions, if not billions, of people to relocate.

Food and water scarcity: Disrupted agricultural patterns, droughts, and floods will exacerbate global hunger and thirst.

Economic collapse: The costs of climate adaptation and mitigation, coupled with extreme weather events, could destabilize economies worldwide.

Conflict and instability: Competition for dwindling resources and mass displacement can fuel social unrest and conflict.

Ecosystem collapse: Climate change is already driving species extinction and ecosystem degradation, which can have cascading effects on human well-being.
